newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea creditors seen pressing for Kia takeover.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea creditors seen pressing for Kia takeover.

text.p: South Korean creditor banks have edged closer to a third-party takeover of the troubled Kia Group by refusing to authorise emergency loans unless group executives agreed to step down, analysts said on Tuesday.
Creditor banks on Monday tempted the eighth-ranked conglomerate with 183.1 billion won ($205.9 million) in emergency loans to four Kia affiliates, including flagship Kia Motors Corp.
But creditors said the loans would be granted only when the group's top executives tendered resignation letters and the labour union agreed in writing to a wage freeze and a workforce reduction.
Creditor banks also agreed to protect Kia Group from going under until September 29. Kia would not be required to service its debts during the protection period.
Kia chairman Kim Sun-hong has steadfastly refused to comply with creditors' demands, while the labour union said it would stop cooperating if management was forced out.
Analysts said the creditors' decision to keep the group afloat while withholding emergency loans would turn up the pressure on Kim.
"I don't think Kia can last more than one month," said James Son, auto analyst at SBC Warburg.
"Pressure will come from many sides. A lot of sub-contractors will experience extreme difficulties, and eventually they will send an SOS to the government and to the creditors."
Kia has an estimated 5,000 sub-contractors
Finance minister Kang Kyong-shik on Tuesday reiterated the government's position that it would not intervene to save Kia or any other troubled group.

"The government has no intention and will never intervene in any takeover bid or industrial restructuring programme," Kang said at a meeting with Kia creditor banks. "The government believes creditors made the right decision and fully supports it."
Analysts welcomed Kang's statements.
"I think it's positive for the restructuring of Korean industry and it will make Korean industry more competitive," said Del Ricks, head of research at BZW Securities.
Lee Jung-ja, head of research at HSBC James Capel, said Kang's comments was a signal that creditor banks would decide Kia's future.
"I think the banking sector wants to sell Kia to a third party. But they want to do it more easily so they are going through a process," Lee said.
"Creditors will continue to pressure management. Without emergency loans I don't think Kia can last more than a week or 10 days."
Kang Hun-sok, auto analyst at ING Barings, believes Kia Motors can survive on its own if it were freed from the burdens of the group's weaker units.
A deal is in the making to sell off two-thirds of Kia Steel, widely viewed as the most burdensome affiliate, to the Hyundai Group and Daewoo groups.
"I think Kia Motors will survive at least in the short-term. The question is whether it can succeed in the medium- or long-term," Kang said.
HSBC Capel's Lee said the long-term problem facing Kia Motors was expected over-capacity in the auto industry if Samsung Group began producing cars as scheduled next March.

The Kia Group, with 38 affiliates at home and abroad, recorded a combined net loss of 129.4 billion won in calendar 1996 on combined sales of 12.1 trillion won. The group's debts were estimated at 9.5 trillion won as of the end of May.
(Conversion: $1 = 889.70)
